lines.text: Say you've just found a new protein, and you want to know what it does.
The quickest way to find out is to find its relatives:
known proteins that look like it, because similar proteins usually do similar jobs.
A carefully checked database called Swiss-Prot holds about five hundred and seventy-six thousand of them.
Comparing yours against every single one, exactly, sounds like a job for a supercomputer.
In this video, we'll do it on this laptop, in about a second,
and we'll see exactly where that speed comes from.
Let's start from the beginning. A protein is a chain of small building blocks called amino acids.
There are twenty kinds, and each one gets a letter,
so a whole protein can be written down as a string of text.
Hemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen in your blood, starts M, V, H, L, T, P,
and runs for a hundred and forty-seven letters.
So how do you measure whether two proteins are similar?
You line them up, letter by letter, and keep a score.
Matching letters earn points, letters that are chemically alike earn a few,
and where one protein has an extra piece, you insert a gap, which costs points.
The best possible line-up gives you the similarity score.
Finding that best line-up exactly is a classic problem, solved by Smith and Waterman in nineteen eighty-one.
You draw a grid, with one protein along the top and the other down the side.
Each cell asks one question: what's the best score that can end right here?
It looks at its neighbours: the diagonal, which adds the score for these two letters,
and the cells above and to the left, which open or extend a gap.
If everything is negative, it simply starts again from zero.
Fill every cell, and the biggest number anywhere in the grid is your answer.
Here's the catch. For a hundred-and-forty-seven-letter query against all of Swiss-Prot,
that grid has thirty point eight billion cells.
A plain C program on one core fills about seven hundred million cells a second,
so a single search takes around forty-three seconds.
Fast tools like BLAST save time by skipping most of the grid,
and they can miss distant relatives. We don't want to skip anything.
The key insight is this: comparing my protein to protein number one tells you nothing about protein number two.
Every comparison is independent, and independent work is exactly what parallel hardware is built for.
This laptop gives us two ways to use it: go wider, and go more.
Wider first. Inside every core are vector registers, two hundred and fifty-six bits wide.
A score fits in sixteen bits, so one register holds sixteen scores side by side.
We give each of those sixteen lanes a different protein from the database,
so a single add instruction moves sixteen grids forward at once.
There's one problem: the lanes move in lockstep, so a batch takes as long as its longest protein.
The fix is simple: sort the database by length, so the proteins in a batch are nearly the same size.
Wasted lanes drop to under a fifth of one percent.
The result: one core goes from point seven one to nine billion cells a second.
That's twelve point seven times faster.
Not quite sixteen, because some work, like loading data and setting up each batch, doesn't get any wider.
Now, go more. This laptop's chip has two kinds of core:
two big performance cores, and eight smaller efficiency cores, each well under half as fast.
If you hand every core an equal share up front, some finish early and sit idle, while one is stuck with the longest proteins.
In our measurements, that cost thirty-one percent more time.
The fix is dynamic scheduling: whenever a core is free, it grabs the next batch,
so every core finishes at the same moment.
We also tried six cleverer schemes. None of them beat that simple rule.
But ten cores still gave only about two and a half times more speed, not ten. Why?
Partly because hyperthreads add nothing here: two threads on one core share the same vector unit, and it's already busy.
And partly because of power. This chip has a fifteen watt limit.
For the first seventeen seconds or so it runs flat out,
then the limit kicks in and every core slows down. Speed drops by forty-one percent.
So on a laptop, how fast your code runs depends on how long it has been running.
Measuring also revealed a surprise. Long queries were twice as slow per cell as short ones.
Their working data no longer fit in each core's tiny, fast L1 cache.
Processing the grid sixteen columns at a time kept it there,
and long queries got one point five four times faster.
Put it all together: twelve point seven times from SIMD, times two point five from threads,
is almost thirty-two times faster than plain C.
And speed is worthless if the answer is wrong, so every score was checked against Parasail, an independent library.
All one point one five million of them matched exactly.
Here's what that looks like for real. This is HySW, running locally in the browser.
We pick hemoglobin beta as the query, and press search.
Each tile is one CPU core: blue for performance cores, orange for efficiency cores,
lit up by the engine's own progress reports.
A moment later, every protein in Swiss-Prot has been scored, and the closest relatives are ranked at the top.
Open a result, and you see the alignment, letter by letter,
and the predicted 3D structure from AlphaFold, with the matching region highlighted.
And the Performance Lab replays each experiment side by side, so you can check every speedup yourself.
So, three lessons. First, look for the independent work. It's what makes parallelism possible.
Second, on mixed cores, hand out work as cores become free, not in equal shares.
And third, on a laptop, power is a resource, so measure it like one.
Exact protein search, on an ordinary laptop, in about a second.
The code, the tests and every raw measurement are on GitHub. Thanks for watching.
